content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Students participate in a historical investigation to further develop their skills and make real-world and personal connections to history. The investigation should extend a particular area of individual student or group interest and be developed to meet students’ learning needs.

The historical concepts and skills content is to be integrated as appropriate.

The Historical investigation focus area is designed to provide students with opportunities to engage in historical inquiry and develop research and communication skills.

Possible historical investigations could include:

  • local or national Aboriginal sites of significance and/or interest
  • the ways sources reveal information about a society, movement, people, groups or events
  • the cause and/or impact of a historical event
  • the significance of a historical development
  • using sources to explain how historical opinions have changed over time for significant people, places or events
  • comparing and contrasting sources with different perspectives
  • the contribution of a historical site or artefact in helping to explain the past
  • perspectives on an individual, group or event over time
  • the accuracy of modern representations of specific historical events
  • an exploration of personal connections such as the contrast between a specific historical society and modern life
  • contemporary issues around preserving or conserving the past, world heritage, tourism, museums, site studies or virtual tours.

web_content_rtb__content.value:
The Modern History 11–12 Syllabus aligns with the Modern History Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus to provide opportunities for integrated delivery.

Through collaborative curriculum planning, it may be decided that Life Skills outcomes and content are the most appropriate option for some students with intellectual disability.

Organisation of Modern History 11–12

Figure 1 shows the organisation of Modern History 11–12.

Image long description: A list of historical concepts and historical skills sits in the middle of the diagram, each surrounded by a box. Historical concepts are: Causation; Continuity and change; Perspectives; Significance; and Contestability. Historical skills are: Analysis and use of sources; Historical interpretation; Historical investigation and research; and Explanation and communication. The syllabus is separated into 3 focus areas for Year 11, and 4 focus areas for Year 12. The focus areas for Year 11 are: Investigating modern history; The shaping of the modern world; and Historical investigation. The focus areas for Year 12 are: Democracy and dictatorship 1919–1939; National studies; Peace and conflict; and Change in the modern world.

Protocols for collaborating with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities

NESA is committed to working in partnership with Aboriginal Communities and supporting teachers, schools and schooling sectors to improve educational outcomes for young people.

It is important to respect appropriate ways of interacting with Aboriginal Communities and Cultural material when teachers plan, program and implement Modern History learning experiences that focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities.

Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) protocols need to be followed. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ICIP protocols include Cultural Knowledges, Cultural Expression and Cultural Property, and documentation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ Identities and lived experiences. It is important to recognise the diversity and complexity of different Cultural groups in NSW, as protocols may differ between local Aboriginal Communities.

Teachers should work in partnership with Elders, parents, Community members, Cultural Knowledge Holders or a local, regional or state Aboriginal Education Consultative Group. It is important to respect Elders and the roles of men and women. Local Aboriginal Peoples should be invited to share their Cultural Knowledges with students and staff when engaging with Aboriginal histories and Cultural Practices.

course_content.name: 📜 Course Description
course_content.value:
Modern History 11–12 focuses on developing student understanding about the history of the world in which they live, and the people, events and forces that have shaped it. The course offers students opportunities to engage with sources from the past, developing their analysis and reasoning skills.

What students learn

Through the study of Modern History 11–12, students learn to:

  • develop an understanding of historical causation and the ways in which human societies have changed over time
  • develop an understanding of the variety of perspectives that have been and are held about the past
  • develop skills in analysis and reasoning to make judgements about the significance of various people and events in the past and form their own conclusions about the nature of historical development
  • construct logical and cogent historical arguments about the past, supported by evidence.

Course structure and requirements

Year 11 course structure and requirements

The Year 11 Modern History course comprises a study of:

  • 120 indicative hours across 3 focus areas.
Year 11 focus areasIndicative hours

Investigating modern history

  • The nature of modern history
  • Case studies

Each case study should be a minimum of 10 indicative hours.

The shaping of the modern world40 (minimum)
Historical investigation20 (maximum)

Content may be integrated across the 3 focus areas of the course in the development of a teaching and learning program.

Investigating modern history

  • The nature of modern history
  • Case studies

Students undertake:

  • at least ONE option from The nature of modern history, AND
  • at least TWO case studies
  • ONE case study must be from Europe, North America or Australia
  • ONE case study must be from Asia, the Pacific, Africa, the Middle East or Central/South America.

The list in the Investigating modern history – Case studies focus area of this syllabus provides case study options teachers may use.

Case studies are investigations into historical features, people, groups, events or concepts in modern history. They are oriented towards the problems and issues of investigating the past.

Case studies in the Year 11 course are intended to provide students with opportunities to:

  • study the various ways historians investigate and construct the past, the types of questions they ask, the explanations they give and the issues they raise
  • question, analyse and interpret sources.

Case studies can provide a historical context in which students learn about relevant methods and issues.

Teachers may develop their own case studies. Case studies must not overlap with or duplicate significantly any option to be attempted in the Year 12 Modern History or History Extension courses.

The shaping of the modern world

Students investigate forces and ideas that shaped the modern world through a study of key events and developments and the meaning of modernity.

At least ONE option from The shaping of the modern world focus area is to be undertaken.

Options selected must not overlap with or duplicate significantly any option to be attempted in the Year 12 Modern History or History Extension courses.

Historical investigation

The Historical investigation is designed to further develop relevant investigative, research and communication skills. The investigation may be undertaken as a standalone study or integrated into any other focus area in the Year 11 course. The investigation should extend a particular area of individual student or group interest. It may be conducted individually or collaboratively.

The investigation must not overlap with or duplicate significantly any option to be attempted in the Year 12 Modern History or History Extension courses.

Historical concepts and skills

The historical concepts and skills content is to be integrated throughout the course. The various studies and options provide the contexts through which concepts and skills are to be developed. These help guide students when engaging in historical analysis and argument.

The Year 12 Modern History course comprises a study of:

  • 120 indicative hours across 4 focus areas.

course_content.name: 📜 Course Description
course_content.value:
Modern History Life Skills 11–12 provides opportunities for students to explore the forces that have shaped the modern world. Students develop skills in locating, selecting, organising, planning and presenting information within a historical context. Students develop knowledge and understanding to contribute as active and informed citizens.

What students learn

Through the study of Modern History Life Skills 11–12, students:

  • explore key events, developments, movements, individuals and groups of the recent past to develop an understanding of how these have impacted our world
  • examine key themes, such as power and authority, nationalism, peace and conflict, and rights and freedoms, and consider how these have contributed to our world
  • develop knowledge and skills in historical inquiry by participating in historical investigations
  • pose questions, gather evidence, process information, draw conclusions and communicate their understandings about the past
  • develop an appreciation of diverse perspectives and ideas.

Course structure

Modern History Life Skills Year 11 and Year 12

The following focus areas can be studied throughout Year 11 (120 hours) and Year 12 (120 hours).

  • Investigating modern history – The nature of modern history; Case studies
  • The shaping of the modern world
  • Historical investigation
  • Democracy and dictatorship 1919–1939
  • National studies
  • Peace and conflict
  • Change in the modern world

For Modern History Life Skills:

  • Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more Modern History Life Skills 11–12 outcomes.
  • Outcomes and content should be selected to meet the particular needs of individual students.
  • The outcomes describe the knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of teaching and learning. Teachers should use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content included in each focus area.
  • The focus areas provide possible frameworks for addressing the Modern History Life Skills 11–12 outcomes and content and are suggestions only. Teachers have the flexibility to select, group and sequence outcomes and content to meet the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of their students.
  • The content for historical concepts and skills should be integrated throughout the course.
  • The Historical investigation can be integrated into any aspect of the course or undertaken as a discrete focus area for students with specific areas of historical interest. The investigation can be undertaken collaboratively or independently. Students can do parts of an investigation or a complete investigation.
  • There is potential for content in Modern History to resonate with students’ lived experiences. Teachers should be aware of the backgrounds and experiences of their students so that they can present different perspectives sensitively.
  • Examples provided in the content are suggestions only. Teachers may use the examples provided or use other examples to meet the particular needs of individual students.
Safety and risk management

Schools are required to ensure they follow safety and risk management in delivering the Modern History Life Skills 11–12 Syllabus.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

Learning about key events or developments in history and responses of individuals and groups to these help students develop an understanding of and manage change in their own lives. Learning about how change can be resisted or supported, and the effects of change on a community provide opportunities for students to consider their own responses to changes in their communities and how to prepare for and respond to these changes.

Students develop self-regulation and self-management skills, an appreciation for diverse perspectives and skills in communicating and sharing ideas.

Designing teaching and learning

Focus of study

One key event or development is selected for study. Consider elements of the content that are appropriate for the key event or development selected.

For example:

  • The Age of Enlightenment – new ways of thinking led people to question the ruling powers. This contributed to the American and French revolutions
  • The French Revolution – how the French commoners advocated for change, including the storming of the Bastille
  • The Age of Imperialism – the expanding control of industrialised countries as they sought raw materials and resources
  • The Industrial Age – the impacts and legacy of the Industrial Revolution
  • The First World War – the experiences of different people, such as soldiers, women and Aboriginal People
  • The Age of Decolonisation – the struggle for independence in a particular country, such as Algeria, Angola, India, Indonesia, Kenya, Rwanda, Suriname, Vietnam.

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching ways in which individuals or groups can gain power, the outcome requires students to recognise causes and effects of events or developments. Students can explore events leading to the French Revolution, such as the financial crisis, poor harvests and anger towards the monarchy. Students match images of events to the results or impacts of these events.

Making connections

Students’ personal backgrounds and family histories will help shape their historical understanding and interpretation. Content in Connections and context can be selected as a starting point for learning about key events or developments that shaped the modern world. For example, when studying the Enlightenment, begin with students identifying new ideas that led to changes in their school community and how people have responded to these changes.

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • Causation – events or actions that led to conflict
  • Significance – legacies from key events or developments.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • The shaping of the modern world: Significance and legacy
    • Short, medium and/or long-term impact of a change
  • Historical concepts and skills: Historical interpretation
    • Make observations about historical impacts and legacy
Teachers use sources to explain the invention of the telephone during the Industrial Revolution. Students recognise how the telephone changed communication between people and communicate how having access to a phone impacts their daily lives.

Connecting with Modern History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Modern History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Modern History syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students may study the same event or development, but the complexity of skills, concepts, sources and level of analysis will differ. For example, when studying WWI, students studying Modern History may explain continuity and change in the nature of warfare, while students studying Modern History Life Skills might identify changes in the ways in which war was fought from WWI to today.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
This teaching advice applies to The shaping of the modern world focus area and is applicable for all options.

The options in The shaping of the modern world explore the historical trends of the past 3 centuries, as well as the meaning of modernity. Learning in this focus area encompasses the key themes of modern thought, significant political and economic change, imperialism, decolonisation and world war.

Students develop targeted historical skills, including the analysis and use of sources, historical interpretation, explanation and communication. Using the discipline-based process of historical inquiry, students analyse sources for evidence, which they then use to develop claims about the past, considering key concepts such as continuity and change, and significance. For the latter, each option contains a content group on significance, which encourages students to consider the importance (or otherwise) of each of the events or movements covered. Using these reasoned claims, students explain and communicate their understanding through historical accounts and arguments.

Designing teaching and learning

Integrating historical concepts and skills: Historical concepts provide the framework through which students develop their understanding of the complexities of the past and the way it has been interpreted through time. They allow students to engage with historical thinking and form their own increasingly perceptive interpretations of historical events, ideas and forces. Teachers select the appropriate concepts on which to focus that align closely with their chosen content options. Some concepts will lend themselves more readily to specific options than others.

Use of sources: Sources are the key to any inquiry into the past and form the basis for historical analysis and interpretation. Using sources, students engage with a variety of perspectives as evidence to inform their understanding of the past. When selecting sources for teaching and learning activities, teachers should use and model ethical practices, such as the consideration of copyright and intellectual property acknowledgement, heritage issues, and Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) concerns, to ensure students understand the importance of engaging appropriately when using historical source material. Select source material carefully to cater for the needs of the students in the class, considering accessibility needs and issues such as the availability of audio and/or closed captions with videos, and of other materials such as tactile objects and replicas of maps and artefacts.

Historical inquiry: Historical inquiry is an active process that allows students to develop and enact the historical skills required to engage with history as a discipline. Through the historical inquiry process, students question, analyse, interpret, explain and communicate their understanding of the past. The historical inquiry process involves students going through the steps of acquiring, processing and communicating in order to demonstrate their application of substantive and conceptual historical understanding.

Teaching and learning activities in The shaping of the modern world should be designed to support students to make evidence-based arguments that explore historical concepts such as causation, significance, and continuity and change. For example, activities which compare and contrast a range of historical sources about an event will support students to engage with these concepts and to develop source-analysis skills. This in turn will encourage more rigorous interpretations. Selecting sources from a wide range of perspectives will develop students’ knowledge base, which will ensure a stronger foundation for analysis and interpretation throughout the focus area.

content.value:
The Historical investigation is designed to provide opportunities for all students to develop the historical skills that are the core of the historical inquiry process. The investigation should extend a particular area of individual student or group interest and be developed to meet students’ learning needs. The investigation can be integrated into any focus area of the Year 11 course. The historical concepts and skills content is to be integrated as appropriate.

The investigation must not overlap with or duplicate significantly any option to be attempted in the Year 12 Modern History or History Extension courses.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Through a focus on the nature of political authority between 1919 and 1939, students investigate the rise of authoritarian, fascist and militarist movements after the First World War, what drew people to these movements, and the regimes that emerged.

Through a study of Germany, students develop an understanding of how a democracy can collapse, the impact of dictatorship on a society, the elimination of individual freedoms, and the threats that dictatorships can pose to peace and security.

When investigating content in the Source analysis content group, students analyse and interpret a range of sources as evidence for the Nazi regime in power from 1933 to 1939.

The historical concepts and skills content is to be integrated as appropriate.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Students participate in a historical investigation to further develop their skills and make real-world and personal connections to history. The investigation should extend a particular area of individual student or group interest and be developed to meet students’ learning needs.

The historical concepts and skills content is to be integrated as appropriate.

The Historical investigation focus area is designed to provide students with opportunities to engage in historical inquiry and develop research and communication skills.

Possible historical investigations could include:

  • local or national Aboriginal sites of significance and/or interest
  • the ways sources reveal information about a society, movement, people, groups or events
  • the cause and/or impact of a historical event
  • the significance of a historical development
  • using sources to explain how historical opinions have changed over time for significant people, places or events
  • comparing and contrasting sources with different perspectives
  • the contribution of a historical site or artefact in helping to explain the past
  • perspectives on an individual, group or event over time
  • the accuracy of modern representations of specific historical events
  • an exploration of personal connections such as the contrast between a specific historical society and modern life
  • contemporary issues around preserving or conserving the past, world heritage, tourism, museums, site studies or virtual tours.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

Learning about a key event or development in history that led to significant change can help students develop an understanding of the impact of individuals, groups and governments on society. Students learn that challenges and struggles can lead to positive change and recognise the power of individuals coming together in enacting change. Students develop an understanding that our lives today are shaped by significant events that have resulted in changes to the modern world.

Students have opportunities to consider how they manage change in their own lives, as well as skills to communicate and share perspectives and understandings about change.

Designing teaching and learning

Focus of study

One key event or development is selected for study. Consider elements of the content appropriate for the event or development selected.

For example:

  • The nuclear age 1945–2021 – nuclear warfare, including the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and the responsibilities of countries in the use of nuclear technology.
  • Civil rights in the United States 1945–1972 – racial segregation and discrimination in the United States and African-American peoples’ fight for rights, including the Montgomery Bus Boycott, the Freedom Rides and activists such as Martin Luther King and Ella Baker.
  • The Anti-Apartheid Movement in South Africa 1948–1994 – the impact of apartheid, the fight against apartheid, including the African National Congress, Nelson Mandela, the Sharpeville Massacre and the Black People’s Convention, and the response of the government.
  • The struggle for democracy in Burma 1948–2021 – Aung San’s fight for democracy and human rights, including the 8888 Uprising.
  • From the Cultural Revolution to Tiananmen Square 1966–1989 – events and impacts of the Cultural Revolution; the fight for democratic reform, including the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests.
  • The changing world order 1989–2016 – changes in the global influence and power of Russia, China and America, including the Tiananmen Square protests, the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Soviet Union, and influences on the global economy; examples in recent history of how politics has appealed to ordinary people, such as the ‘Brexit’ referendum, the election of Donald Trump, the influence of Viktor Orbán.

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching about Nelson Mandela’s role in the Anti-Apartheid Movement in South Africa, the outcome requires students to investigate people, events or developments of the modern world. Students can be guided to locate information in sources to answer teacher-developed key inquiry questions and draw conclusions about the significance of Nelson Mandela in the collapse of apartheid.

Making connections

Students’ personal backgrounds and family histories will help shape their historical understanding and interpretation. Content in Connections and context can be selected as a starting point for learning about key events or developments that led to change. For example, students can begin by identifying key changes in their own life and how their own actions and decisions either led to or shaped the change. They can consider how they respond to change, as well as recognise responses to change that affects groups of people, such as a change in a school rule, or a change to facilities or infrastructure in the local community.

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • Causation – reasons for resistance or opposition to an event, government or movement
  • Perspectives – diverse perspectives of groups of people during a particular event or development, for example perspectives of African-American people, white people and the government during the Freedom Rides.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • Change in the modern world: The nature and development of a historical conflict
    • Significant movements associated with the change
  • Historical concepts and skills: Historical investigation and research
    • Pose question(s) about the past

When learning about the Tiananmen Square protests, the teacher provides visual sources for students to examine. Students are provided with a scaffold to pose a question based on what they observe in the source, for example, ‘Why were so many people there?’, ‘Why are they mostly young people?’.


Connecting with Modern History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Modern History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Modern History syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students may study the same key event or development, but the complexity of skills, concepts, sources and level of analysis will differ. For example, when studying the Nuclear Age, students studying Modern History may analyse the perspectives of different groups on uranium mining, such as environmental groups, indigenous people and governments, while students studying Modern History Life Skills might identify the benefits and challenges of uranium mining.

Purpose

Understanding who holds power or authority in a community and how power or authority is gained can help students develop an understanding of the difference between democracy and dictatorships. Students are able to identify how the Nazi Party gained power and the impacts this had. This enables students to consider how power and authority can be used within a community and their own agency in relation to making decisions in their lives.

Designing teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching about the rise of the Nazi Party, the outcome requires students to describe features of places or societies in the modern world. Students engage with a range of sources that illustrate what life was like in Germany in the 1930s and select or compose descriptive words or phrases to describe the experiences of citizens.

Making connections

Students’ personal backgrounds and family histories will help shape their historical understanding and interpretation. Content in Connections and context can be selected as a starting point for learning about democracy and dictatorship. For example, students can identify positions of power or authority in familiar contexts and ways in which people respond to power or authority before exploring the actions of the Nazi Party.

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • Perspectives – the perspectives of citizens, soldiers, youth and Jewish people
  • Causation – how the Nazi Party gained power.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • Democracy and dictatorship: The Nazi regime in power 1933–1939
    • Main ideas of Nazi ideology
  • Historical concepts and skills: Analysis and use of sources
    • Organise information from sources
Students engage with a range of sources to locate information about Nazi beliefs and ideology. They use a graphic organiser to organise the evidence from sources into categories such as discrimination, superiority, power.

Connecting with Modern History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Modern History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Modern History syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students can study the concepts of democracy and dictatorship, and the Nazi regime, but the complexity of skills, concepts, sources and level of analysis will differ. For example, when exploring methods of control used by the Nazi regime, students studying Modern History may assess the impacts of different methods, while students studying Modern History Life Skills might engage with an example of propaganda and draw conclusions about the effect this had on the German people.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

Engaging in a historical investigation enables students to develop critical thinking skills as they determine what information is useful and reliable, and use that information to support an opinion or argument. When working collaboratively with others, students can build interpersonal skills such as empathy, appreciation of diverse perspectives and the ability to share opinions and ideas.

Designing teaching and learning

This focus area can be integrated into any aspect of the Modern History Life Skills course to further explore an area of interest. A student may complete all, part or selected aspects of an investigation. The investigation can be done as a class, in small groups or independently.

The historical inquiry process is central to the historical investigation and is articulated in the content groups. The steps include:

  • posing and responding to a question about the past
  • gathering primary and secondary sources of evidence
  • processing and analysing information
  • drawing conclusions
  • communicating understanding.

In addition to this, students may need to consolidate their understanding of history through personal connections before beginning the historical inquiry process.

Historical concepts and skills

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate. Understanding the concept of perspective, for example is critical to determining which source material is useful and reliable.

Historical skills should be integrated and may be selected to meet the individual needs of students. For example, one student might focus on placing events related to the investigation in chronological order while another student finds important information about an event.

Selecting a historical investigation

The scope and nature of the investigation can be adjusted to align with the student’s strengths, interests, needs and goals, or to overlap with another focus area.

Teaching and learning strategies

Explicit teaching

  • Teach students to first order events according to the year. Next order events within the same year by month and then date.
  • Provide modelled, guided and independent practice in locating historical sources online by determining keywords for a search and selecting a reliable website from the search results.

Scaffolds

  • Provide a template for students to use to organise information from sources, including where it is from, when it originated, who the author or creator is, why it was written or made, and what information it conveys.
  • Provide students with a graphic organiser to support their communication of continuity and change within the investigation, such as a Venn diagram or T-chart.

Feedback

  • Provide students with explicit feedback to direct and redirect the inquiry. For example, provide feedback to help students formulate inquiry questions that will provide enough scope for an investigation without being too broad.
  • Provide explicit feedback on when and how to use historical terms and concepts.

Connecting with Modern History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Modern History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Modern History syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students can participate in a historical investigation, but the scope of the investigation and the amount of scaffolding and support provided will differ. For example, students studying Modern History locate sources independently, while students studying Modern History Life Skills may select from a curated set of sources targeted to their level of understanding.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

Exploring historic sites and sources enables students to develop the skills needed to learn about the past. When engaging with artefacts, images and stories, students develop an understanding that people, places and events can be interpreted and represented in different ways. Students develop interpersonal skills such as empathy and appreciation for diverse perspectives, including ethical perspectives relating to the ownership of sites, artefacts and sources.

Designing teaching and learning

The Investigating modern history focus area consists of 2 parts – The nature of modern history and Case studies. The nature of modern history introduces students to the nature and use of historic sites and sources. Students can then apply their learning to Case studies.

Focus of study

Content for study can be selected in the following ways.

Selecting a single option for study from The nature of modern history. For example:

  • The investigation of historic sites and sources, e.g. Life in The Rocks in the 19th century, North Head Quarantine Station, the nature of trench warfare in the First World War.
  • The contestability of the past, e.g. John Simpson and his donkey, Hitler’s diaries, Pearl Harbor – a surprise attack?
  • The construction of modern histories, e.g. the mutiny on the Bounty, the Holocaust, a historical individual such as Eva Perón, Che Guevara, Nicholas II, Charles Perkins.
  • The representation and commemoration of the past, e.g. the Yasukuni Shrine, the Sydney Jewish Museum and survivor testimony, a historical film or website, Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander oral histories.

Selecting 2 or more options for study from The nature of modern history. For example:

  • The investigation of historic sites and sources: Storing and archiving records, and The contestability of the past: Limitations and reliability of sources
  • The contestability of the past: Contestability, and The construction of modern histories: Construction and reconstruction.

Selecting one option from The nature of modern history AND one option from Case studies. For example:

  • The representation and commemoration of the past, and Pemulwuy
  • The investigation of historic sites and sources, and The transatlantic slave trade
  • The investigation of historic sites and sources, and Women’s movements
  • The contestability of the past, and The decline and fall of the Romanov dynasty
  • The contestability of the past, and Contact in the Pacific
  • The contestability of the past, and The New Zealand (Māori) Wars
  • The construction of modern histories, and Empress Dowager Cixi

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching about how sources can provide different interpretations of the past, the outcome requires students to identify different interpretations. Students engage with American and Japanese recounts of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor and select words or write a sentence to identify how the events were interpreted in each recount (e.g. surprise attack / well planned; sneaky / strategic; devastating / victory).

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • Perspectives, significance and contestability – whose perspectives are represented in sources? How reliable are sites and sources in giving us information about the past?

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • The construction of modern histories: Construction and reconstruction
    • Ways in which history is preserved or conserved, including personal or community history
  • Historical concepts and skills: Analysis and use of sources
    • Locate, select and organise a range of sources that are records of own personal history
Students identify a range of sources that provide information about key events and developments in their own lives. They select the most relevant sources and display them either physically or digitally to ‘tell the story’ of their lives. They explain the origin and chronology of the sources using historical terms.

Connecting with Modern History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Modern History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Modern History syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students may study the same option within Investigating modern history, but the depth and scope of content will differ. For example, when studying The representation and commemoration of the past option, students studying Modern History may analyse sources to explain different representations of the past and how this has influenced commemorations, while students studying Modern History Life Skills might identify the significance of a historical event in Australia’s history and ways in which we commemorate this event.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

Through the study of a selected nation, students develop an understanding of how leaders and governments can support a society, as well as reasons why leaders and governments may be opposed. Students develop an appreciation for the ways in which our lives today can be shaped by individuals, governments and events of the past.

Students develop skills in time and chronology when they explore significant events in a nation’s history as well as empathy for diverse perspectives and interpretations of people and events.

Designing teaching and learning

Focus of study

One national study is selected for study. Consider elements of the content appropriate for the national study selected.

For example:

  • Australia 1918–1949 – changes in society after the First World War, including the changing roles of women and Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Peoples; the cause and effects of the Great Depression; Australian nationalism and Aboriginal activism in the 1930s
  • China 1927–1949 – the rise and impact of the Chinese Communist Party; Japanese invasions
  • Cuba 1940–1991 – the Cuban Revolution, including the roles of Fidel Castro and Che Guevara
  • Indonesia 1945–2004 – the influence of the Indonesian Communist Party and the 1965 coup; Suharto and the power of the military
  • Iran 1945–1989 – Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi’s power and authority; Iran’s relationship with the West, including the significance of oil and the hostage crisis
  • Japan 1904–1937 – the modernisation of Japan through industrialisation and strengthening of the military; the tension between tradition and modernisation
  • Russia and the Soviet Union 1917–1941 – Stalin’s rise to power and the Stalinist regime
  • United States 1919–1941 – the Great Depression and its impacts; growth in industrialisation and American consumerism prior to the Second World War.

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching about the Great Depression and its impacts on Australia, the outcome requires students to identify continuity and change in the modern world. The teacher uses sources to provide students with first-hand accounts of the Great Depression and students identify ways the government responds to unemployment today as a result of these events.

Making connections

Students’ personal backgrounds and family histories will help shape their historical understanding and interpretation. Content in Connections and context can be selected as a starting point for learning about how individuals, groups and events can shape the history of a nation. For example, students can recognise authority and leadership in familiar contexts, before identifying how authority and leadership is beneficial for groups and communities and finally how groups and communities can influence authority and leadership.

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • Causation – causes of significant events in a nation’s history and the effects of the event
  • Continuity and change – how particular events or individuals have led to changes in a selected nation
  • Perspectives – the perspectives of different groups of people to a significant event in a nation’s history, for example workers, government, women.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • National studies: Events and developments
    • An event that has shaped the selected nation
  • Historical concepts and skills: Historical interpretation
    • Recognise the causes of events or developments in the past
    • Recognise the effects of events or developments in the past
After learning about the Shah of Iran and how his leadership was opposed, the teacher uses sources to outline the events of the hostage crisis. Students use a graphic organiser to represent key events leading to the hostage crisis. Using a sentence stem, students record one effect of the hostage crisis on Iran’s relationship with the US.

Connecting with Modern History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Modern History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Modern History syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students may study the same national study, but the complexity of skills, concepts, sources and level of analysis will differ. For example, when studying the United States, students studying Modern History may assess the role and significance of American consumerism to the economic and social growth of the US, while students studying Modern History Life Skills might investigate changes to the US film industry during the period.

Purpose

Exploring a significant conflict in history can help students develop from a personal understanding of conflict to a broader understanding of conflict between groups, communities and countries. Learning about causes of and responses to a particular conflict can provide opportunities for students to consider conflict resolution in a range of contexts. Students develop an appreciation and empathy for diverse perspectives, skills in time and chronology as they sequence events of a particular conflict, as well as communication skills as they share ideas and understandings.

Designing teaching and learning

Focus of study

One event is selected for study. Consider elements of the content appropriate for the event selected.

For example:

  • Conflict in Europe 1935–1945 – campaigns of the Second World War throughout Europe, such as German occupation, the Battle of Britain, the Battle of Stalingrad, the Siege of Tobruk
  • Conflict in the Pacific 1937–1951 – Japanese campaigns, such as the attack on Pearl Harbor, the Battle of the Coral Sea and the atomic bomb
  • The Cold War 1945–1991 – rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, the arms race and the space race, the division between East and West Berlin including the Berlin Wall, the Vietnam War
  • The Arab–Israeli conflict 1948–2000 – conflict between Israel and neighbouring Arab countries, such as the Six-Day War, the Yom Kippur War and responses such as the intifadas and Hamas
  • Conflict in Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos 1954–1976 – the fight for communism by North Vietnam, China and the USSR
  • Conflict in the Gulf 1980–2017 – the regime of Saddam Hussein, the first Gulf War, including Operation Desert Shield and Operation Desert Storm and the 9/11 attacks.

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching about the nature and development of the Six-Day War, the outcome requires students to investigate people, events or developments of the modern world. As a class, students can be guided to develop key inquiry questions, engage with relevant sources, locate information and draw conclusions about the consequences of the conflict on civilians.

Making connections

Students’ personal backgrounds and family histories will help shape their historical understanding and interpretation. Content in Connections and context can be selected as a starting point for learning about peace and conflict. For example, students reflect on conflicts that can arise in a familiar environment, such as family, school or workplace and identify reasons for conflict, why conflicts are difficult to resolve and peaceful ways to resolve conflict.

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • Causation – reasons for a particular conflict, including key events that led to the conflict
  • Significance and contestability – representations of a particular conflict and the impacts or consequences for groups of people, including nations.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • Peace and conflict: The nature and development of a historical conflict
    • Chronology of key events in the conflict
  • Historical concepts and skills: Time and chronology
    • Use chronology to order people, places, changes and events from the past
Students order key events in the German occupation throughout Europe by arranging events in order or creating a timeline. The teacher models ordinal language and students use this language to describe the order of events.

Connecting with Modern History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Modern History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Modern History syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students may study the same conflict, but the complexity of skills, concepts, sources and level of analysis will differ. For example, when studying the Cold War, students studying Modern History may propose arguments about the causes and effects of the erection of the Berlin Wall, while students studying Modern History Life Skills might recognise how lives of people in East Berlin changed as a result of the Berlin Wall.

Purpose

Learning about key events or developments in history and responses of individuals and groups to these help students develop an understanding of and manage change in their own lives. Learning about how change can be resisted or supported, and the effects of change on a community provide opportunities for students to consider their own responses to changes in their communities and how to prepare for and respond to these changes.

Students develop self-regulation and self-management skills, an appreciation for diverse perspectives and skills in communicating and sharing ideas.

Designing teaching and learning

Focus of study

One key event or development is selected for study. Consider elements of the content that are appropriate for the key event or development selected.

For example:

  • The Age of Enlightenment – new ways of thinking led people to question the ruling powers. This contributed to the American and French revolutions
  • The French Revolution – how the French commoners advocated for change, including the storming of the Bastille
  • The Age of Imperialism – the expanding control of industrialised countries as they sought raw materials and resources
  • The Industrial Age – the impacts and legacy of the Industrial Revolution
  • The First World War – the experiences of different people, such as soldiers, women and Aboriginal People
  • The Age of Decolonisation – the struggle for independence in a particular country, such as Algeria, Angola, India, Indonesia, Kenya, Rwanda, Suriname, Vietnam.

Outcomes and content

Outcomes are concise statements of the essential knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of the teaching and learning of the syllabus. For example, when teaching ways in which individuals or groups can gain power, the outcome requires students to recognise causes and effects of events or developments. Students can explore events leading to the French Revolution, such as the financial crisis, poor harvests and anger towards the monarchy. Students match images of events to the results or impacts of these events.

Making connections

Students’ personal backgrounds and family histories will help shape their historical understanding and interpretation. Content in Connections and context can be selected as a starting point for learning about key events or developments that shaped the modern world. For example, when studying the Enlightenment, begin with students identifying new ideas that led to changes in their school community and how people have responded to these changes.

Historical concepts

One or more historical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

For example:

  • Causation – events or actions that led to conflict
  • Significance – legacies from key events or developments.

Historical skills

Historical skills should be integrated into teaching and learning activities.

For example:

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities
  • The shaping of the modern world: Significance and legacy
    • Short, medium and/or long-term impact of a change
  • Historical concepts and skills: Historical interpretation
    • Make observations about historical impacts and legacy
Teachers use sources to explain the invention of the telephone during the Industrial Revolution. Students recognise how the telephone changed communication between people and communicate how having access to a phone impacts their daily lives.

Connecting with Modern History 11–12

Teachers may be programming Modern History Life Skills content integrated with content from the Modern History syllabus to meet the needs of students accessing different courses in the same class. All students may study the same event or development, but the complexity of skills, concepts, sources and level of analysis will differ. For example, when studying WWI, students studying Modern History may explain continuity and change in the nature of warfare, while students studying Modern History Life Skills might identify changes in the ways in which war was fought from WWI to today.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
The content groups Context and Interwar dictatorships provide students with an understanding of the key reasons for the rise of dictatorships in the interwar period and prepare students for their study of Germany from 1919 to 1939 in the broader political and diplomatic context. The themes of authoritarianism, fascism and militarism can be useful in framing this content. By then applying this conceptual understanding to 2 specific dictatorships, students can draw connections between cause and effect. The 2 dictatorships selected can be taught concurrently to show similarities or differences in their emergence. Germany cannot be selected as one of these dictatorships.

The intent of the remaining content is for students to learn about:

  • the collapse of democracy in Germany, and the establishment and development of the Nazi dictatorship, focusing on the methods of control, including ideology and the cult of personality
  • the impact on a range of groups, including those who conformed or benefited
  • opposition and resistance to the regime.

Democracy and dictatorship 1919–1939 is not intended to be a study of the build-up to the Second World War.

Students develop targeted historical skills including the analysis and use of sources, historical interpretation, explanation and communication. Using the discipline-based process of historical inquiry, students analyse sources for evidence, which they then use to develop claims about the past, considering key concepts such as perspectives and contestability. Using these reasoned claims, students explain and communicate their understanding through historical accounts and arguments.

Teachers should provide a range of different types of sources, primary and secondary, so that students can apply and further develop the source-analysis skills learnt in Year 11. Providing a range of sources of varied complexity allows all students, including those with diverse learning needs, to engage in the process of analysis and historical inquiry.

Designing teaching and learning

Integrating historical concepts and skills: Historical concepts provide the framework through which students develop their understanding of the complexities of the past and the way it has been interpreted through time. They allow students to engage with historical thinking and form their own increasingly perceptive interpretations of historical events, ideas and forces. Teachers select the appropriate concepts on which to focus that align closely with their chosen content options. Some concepts will lend themselves more readily to specific options than others.

Use of sources: Sources are the key to any inquiry into the past and form the basis for historical analysis and interpretation. Using sources, students engage with a variety of perspectives as evidence to inform their understanding of the past. When selecting sources for teaching and learning activities, teachers should use and model ethical practices, such as the consideration of copyright and intellectual property acknowledgement, heritage issues, and Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) concerns, to ensure students understand the importance of engaging appropriately when using historical source material. Select source material carefully to cater for the needs of the students in the class, considering accessibility needs and issues such as the availability of audio and/or closed captions with videos, and of other materials such as tactile objects and replicas of maps and artefacts.

Historical inquiry: Historical inquiry is an active process that allows students to develop and enact the historical skills required to engage with history as a discipline. Through the historical inquiry process, students question, analyse, interpret, explain and communicate their understanding of the past. The historical inquiry process involves students going through the steps of acquiring, processing and communicating in order to demonstrate their application of substantive and conceptual historical understanding.

Teaching and learning activities in Democracy and dictatorship 1919–1939 should be designed to support students to make evidence-based arguments that explore historical concepts such as causation, significance, and continuity and change. For example, activities which compare and contrast a range of historical sources about an event will support students to engage with these concepts and to develop source-analysis skills. This in turn will encourage more rigorous interpretations. Selecting sources from a wide range of perspectives will develop students’ knowledge base, which will ensure a stronger foundation for analysis and interpretation throughout the focus area.

web_content_rtb__content.name: 📜 Content
web_content_rtb__content.value:
Assessment is used to analyse and interpret the knowledge, understanding and skills that students demonstrate throughout the learning process. Assessment provides information about student learning and achievement at a point in time and the progress students have made.

Assessment is most effective when it is an integral part of teaching and learning. The primary role of assessment is to identify where students are in their learning so that teaching can be adapted to target student needs, and progress can be monitored over time.

Schools use syllabuses, assessment and reporting materials and Assessment Certification and Examination (ACE) requirements to develop school-based assessment programs.

Assessment involves:

  •  identifying where students are in their learning
  •  ongoing monitoring of student progress in relation to the syllabus
  •  providing feedback about student progress to determine the next steps in learning.

Effective school-based assessment:

  • enables students to demonstrate what they know, understand and can do
  • is inclusive of, and accessible for, all students
  • is valid: there is clear alignment between the syllabus, the assessment activity and the criteria used to assess
  • identifies strengths, misunderstandings and skills not yet mastered
  • enables timely and relevant feedback about learning progress
  • provides opportunities for students to reflect on feedback
  • is regular, purposeful and integrated throughout teaching and learning
  • informs goal setting for learning and teaching.

Teachers should evaluate the effectiveness of their assessment approaches regularly to ensure they are fit for purpose. Reviewing student work in relation to assessment activities can provide useful information for decision-making.

Decisions teachers make about teaching, learning and assessment include:

  • what outcomes will be assessed in relation to the content that has been taught
  • why assessment will occur at a point in time and for what purpose
  • how information about student learning will be gathered and what approach will be used
  • how the information will be used, including to provide feedback, and to determine student progress and achievement
  • what next steps will inform future teaching and learning.

Standards-referenced assessment

Standards-referenced assessment refers to the process of interpreting information about student learning in relation to standards. It is used to compare student performance to a standard with objective criteria rather than to the performance of other students. Standards-referenced assessment can provide meaningful feedback about student achievement and support consistent assessment and reporting.

What are standards?

A standards-referenced approach is used to assess and report student achievement in NSW. This approach comprises 2 components:

  • syllabus outcomes and content describe what students are expected to learn
  • how well students demonstrate achievement is described in performance standards such as the Common Grade Scale.

Syllabus outcomes are used by teachers to:

  • plan and develop learning and assessment opportunities in relation to content
  • assess student progress and achievement in relation to intended learning
  • report student progress and achievement at key points in time.

Performance standards used to report student achievement in NSW include:

  • Common Grade Scale (Years 1 to 10)
  • Stage 5 Course Performance Descriptors (end of Year 10)
  • Common Grade Scale for preliminary courses (Year 11)
  • HSC Performance Band Descriptions (Year 12)
  • achievement level descriptions (Year 12 English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1, and Numeracy).

It is not a requirement for student reports in Early Stage 1 to refer to a performance standard such as a grade scale. More information on standards-referenced reporting is available in Reporting and using grades.

Inclusive assessment

Approaches to assessment should be inclusive of all students. Assessment design should consider the ways students engage in the activity, how information is presented and accessed, and the different ways that students can demonstrate their understanding. Inclusive assessment means ensuring all students are able to demonstrate their learning.

Inclusive assessment considers the following:

  • How students engage:
    • developing accessible learning goals and criteria
    • integrating student choice, for example allowing students to choose topics or contexts in which they demonstrate learning
    • simulating real-life contexts that have explicit relevance to students.
  • How information is presented and accessed, including:
    • resources and/or stimulus material that is presented across a range of modes and that include accessibility options
    • both digital and non-digital resources.
  • How students respond:
    • using self-paced activities that support students to demonstrate learning without time constraints
    • providing opportunities for students to make choices about how they communicate their learning
    • providing opportunities to challenge and/or extend students within their level of understanding.

Adjustments for students with disability

It is a requirement under the Disability Standards for Education 2005 for schools to ensure that assessment tasks are accessible to students with disability. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access assessment activities and tasks and to demonstrate their learning. In some cases, this may mean providing an alternative assessment activity. Schools are responsible for any decisions made at school level to offer adjustments to assessment activities and tasks, including in-school tests. Decisions regarding adjustments should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

Checking grades involves reviewing the history of grades allocated by a school to analyse patterns and clarify grading decisions.

When making comparisons, teachers should ensure their grading decisions are based on all available assessment information referenced by relevant grade scales or performance descriptors and published standards.

Schools can use the Grade History Function in Schools Online or the Results Analysis Package to view the grades they have allocated in each course.

Schools can monitor their grade patterns by comparing them to other available data about the performance of students at their school. This will enable schools to have confidence that the grades they intend to allocate are consistent with what they expected from a particular cohort or group of students completing a course.

Principals are accountable for the pattern of grades allocated by their school at the end of Stage 5 and Year 11 courses (except Life Skills and VET) and Year 12 English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1 and Numeracy CEC. Principals (or their delegates) need to confirm that grades are consistent with published standards when they are submitted.

Determining grades

A standards-referenced approach is used to report student achievement in NSW. Achievement standards are based on what students are expected to learn and how well they have achieved.

The NSW syllabuses state the intended learning for students by the end of each stage. A to E grade scales describe how well students have achieved. Teachers make professional on-balance judgements to decide which grade description best matches the standards their students have achieved at a particular point in time. These decisions are based on evidence of achievement and information teachers have collected during the teaching and learning.

The A to E grade allocated to a student and reported on NESA credentials reflects the level of achievement demonstrated by the student at the end of the course.

Moderating grades

Teachers follow a process of ‘moderation’ to ensure that grades allocated are consistent with published standards. This means that the grade a student receives in one school can be compared to the same grade anywhere in NSW.

Teachers moderate their judgements by comparing work samples for their students with samples aligned to grades A to E.

Choosing the right grade

Reporting with grades requires that teachers use on-balance judgement in relation to standards. This is a key professional skill.

An on-balance judgement does not just focus on a single piece of work or solely on test results.

Teachers should weigh up the evidence of achievement and other information collected for a student up to that point in time. This information is derived from learning activities, observations and other methods of assessment that are collected over time and in different situations. For further information read our Assessment principles page.

Making on-balance professional judgments involves considering all available evidence of student achievement, with an emphasis on identifying the descriptors that best reflect each student’s performance by the end of the course. Relying solely on marks and predetermined cut scores to allocate grades can lead to inaccuracies, especially for students who demonstrate significant progress over time and are performing at a higher level at the course’s conclusion than they were earlier in the course.

Students with disability

Students with disability may require adjustments to assessment activities to enable access to the activities and equitable opportunity to demonstrate what they know and can do. Students with disability who receive adjustments to assessment activities should have access to the full range of grades.

Using student work samples

Schools can use student work samples to strengthen their understanding of standards. NESA provides limited work samples aligned to A to E grades for a selection of learning areas to assist teachers in understanding state-wide standards. Available work samples can be found with the syllabuses.

Schools can use these published work samples to moderate the grades they allocate to students by comparing the standards of work published with those produced by their students in the same or similar learning areas.

Schools can also use samples of work from their own students for professional development with their staff and/or teachers from other schools. These work samples can provide the basis for professional discussions about standards and ensure there are consistent expectations about student achievement in relation to syllabus outcomes.

Reviewing and improving assessment activities

Referring to student work from previous years may assist teachers to clarify what is expected prior to the grading or marking of student work. Reviewing student work samples may also provide useful information about assessment activities that could lead to improvements in task design. For example, if an assessment activity is found to provide limited opportunities for students to demonstrate achievement at grade A, this could inform future assessment activities so that they are designed with increased scope for students to demonstrate higher levels of knowledge, understanding and skills in relation to the relevant grade scale or achievement level descriptions.

Determining Stage 5 grades

Assessing student achievement is the process of collecting information on student performance in relation to the objectives and outcomes of a course.

In setting activities or tasks, teachers should give careful consideration to the syllabus objectives and outcomes being assessed. By measuring student achievement in relation to these objectives and outcomes, teachers can build up a profile of the achievement of each student in relation to the course performance descriptors.

Grading student achievement is the process of assigning a letter (A, B, C, D, E) to summarise the level of a student's achievement in a course. For students undertaking courses without subject-specific course performance descriptors, that is, Board Endorsed or Content Endorsed Courses, a grade from A to E should be assigned using the Common Grade Scale.

Establishing an assessment program

In establishing an assessment program, teachers should ensure that the types of assessment activities or tasks used are appropriate to the objectives and outcomes being assessed. Generally, it will be necessary to use a number of different assessment activities or tasks in order to ensure that student achievement in relation to all the knowledge and skills objectives is assessed. Principals have the authority to decide on and to implement disability provisions for school-based assessments and tests.

The assessment program should also reflect the relative emphasis placed on the assessable objectives of school programs and the syllabus. For example, where a school has placed considerable emphasis on the development of research skills, that emphasis should be reflected in the assessment program. Objectives from the affective domain (i.e. values and attitudes) should not be used in determining a student's grade.

Where activities or tasks are scheduled throughout a course, greater weight would generally be given to those activities or tasks undertaken towards the end of the course. For example, in a 200-hour course extending over Years 9 and 10, the assessment information collected in Year 10 provides the more complete picture of student achievement. There are, however, a number of different ways of organising the teaching/learning program for a course. The scheduling of activities or tasks and the weights applied should reflect the course organisation. Students should be given the opportunity to demonstrate their maximum level of achievement relative to the course performance descriptors.

Applying the course performance descriptors

Course performance descriptors have been developed for each course. They describe the main features of a typical student's performance at each grade measured against the syllabus objectives and outcomes for the course.

Teachers will make the final judgement of the most appropriate grade on the basis of all available assessment information and with reference to the course performance descriptors. In applying these descriptors, teachers should interpret them in terms of standards that can be achieved by Stage 5 students within the bounds of the course. The same course performance descriptors apply to 100-hour and 200-hour courses. This relates to courses studied across Years 9 and 10, and to courses studied exclusively in either Year 9 or Year 10.

The grades allocated should reflect the relative emphasis placed on the assessable objectives of school programs and the syllabus. For example, where a school has placed considerable emphasis on the development of research skills, that emphasis should be reflected in the assessment program. Objectives from the affective domain (i.e. values and attitudes) should not be used in determining a student's grade.

Advice for Year 12: English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1 and Numeracy CEC

Schools must allocate to students who complete Year 12 English Studies or Mathematics Standard 1, or Numeracy CEC the grade that reflects their achievement at the end of the course. This grade is reported on the student’s HSC Record of Achievement.

To ensure grades have consistent meaning across the state, NESA monitors the grades allocated and reviews student work samples provided by schools.

Checklist for schools

This checklist relates to Year 12 grades that are reported on students' NESA credentials.

1. Read the Achievement Level Descriptions

Familiarise yourself with the Achievement Level Descriptions, on the syllabus page for the relevant course.

  • English Studies Achievement Level Descriptions
  • Mathematics Standard 1 Achievement Level Descriptions
  • Numeracy CEC Achievement Level Descriptions

2. Review work samples

Samples of student work aligned to grades are provided on the syllabus page. Use the samples and their annotations to get a clear understanding of the standard at each grade.

3. Upload grades and work samples

  • Decide on the appropriate grade for each student based on the achievement they have demonstrated at the end of the course.
  • Enter student grades in Schools Online.
  • Upload student work samples and the associated assessment activities in Schools Online.

Schools Online has guides on how to enter grades and upload student work samples. Learn more about submitting work samples.

4. Confirm grades

Check the grades entered in Schools Online are correct before they are confirmed by the principal.

5. Revise grades

Schools may be contacted by NESA and asked to revise grades. If your school is contacted, you will have a short period of time to make changes.

6. Keep grades confidential

NESA monitors grades before they are finalised and released to students. School assessment grades are available to students in Students Online once the final HSC exam has ended. Do not reveal grades to students before this time.
